message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Properties**

| Category | Property | Typical Value / Description |
|----------|----------|-----------------------------|
| **Basic Identity** | Symbol | H |
| | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium), ³H (tritium) |
| | State at STP | Gas (colorless, odorless, tasteless) |
| | Boiling point | –252.9 °C (−423.2 °F) |
| | Melting point | –259.2 °C (−434.6 °F) |
| | Density (gas, 0 °C, 1 atm) | 0.0899 g L⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume (ideal gas) | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV |
| | Electron affinity | 0.754 eV |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | First ionization energy | 13.598 eV |
| | Second ionization energy | 27.211 eV |
| | Heat capacity (gas, 25 °C) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Specific heat ratio (γ) | 1.41 (diatomic) |
| | Speed of sound (in H₂) | ~1270 m s⁻¹ at 20 °C |
| | Refractive index (visible) | 1.000132 |
| | Solubility in water | ~1.6 g L⁻¹ at 25 °C |
| | Solubility in ethanol | ~10 g L⁻¹ at 25 °C |
| | Vapor pressure (at 25 °C) | 1.3 kPa |
| | Boiling point of isotopes | ¹H: –252.9 °C; ²H: –246.0 °C; ³H: –246.0 °C |
| | Fusion energy (nuclear) | 17.6 MeV per reaction (p + d → ³He + γ) |
| **Chemical Behavior** | Bonding | Forms covalent bonds; diatomic H₂ is the most common form. |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (e.g., H⁺), –1 (e.g., hydride H⁻). |
| | Acidic behavior | Acts as a proton donor (H⁺) in acids. |
| | Basic behavior | Acts as a hydride donor (H⁻) in bases. |
| | Redox potential | Standard reduction potential of H⁺/H₂: 0 V (vs SHE). |
| | Reactivity | Highly reactive with many elements; forms hydrides, oxides, halides, etc. |
| | Combustion | H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O (exothermic, 286 kJ mol⁻¹). |
| | Catalytic role | Used in catalytic hydrogenation reactions. |
| | Electrolysis | Splits water into H₂ and O₂; requires ~1.23 V (thermodynamic). |
| **Physical & Spectroscopic** | Spectral lines | Lyman series (UV), Balmer series (visible), Paschen series (IR). |
| | Rotational spectrum | Microwave region; used in radio astronomy. |
| | Vibrational frequency (H₂) | ~4401 cm⁻¹ (infrared). |
| | Magnetic moment | 1.410 MHz/T (proton NMR). |
| | Nuclear spin | ½ (proton). |
| | Hyperfine splitting | 1420 MHz (21 cm line) – key in astrophysics. |
| **Applications & Uses** | Fuel cell fuel | H₂ + O₂ → H₂O (electricity). |
| | Rocket propellant | Liquid H₂ + liquid O₂ (high specific impulse). |
| | Metallurgy | Reducing agent for metal extraction. |
| | Chemical synthesis | Hydrogenation, ammonia synthesis (Haber–Bosch). |
| | Medical imaging | Deuterated solvents for NMR. |
| | Energy storage | Hydrogen storage in metal hydrides, high‑pressure tanks. |
| | Scientific research | Calibration of spectrometers, fundamental physics tests. |
| **Safety & Handling** | Flammability | Extremely flammable; lower explosive limit ~4 % in air. |
| | Toxicity | Non‑toxic, but can cause asphyxiation in confined spaces. |
| | Storage | Requires high‑pressure cylinders or cryogenic tanks. |
| | Environmental impact | Zero CO₂ emissions when combusted; but production often fossil‑fuel‑based. |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Protium (¹H) | Most abundant (~99.98 %). |
| | Deuterium (²H) | Stable, 0.015 % natural abundance; used in heavy water. |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (half‑life 12.32 y); used in nuclear fusion research. |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Hydrogen is the simplest element**: one proton, one electron, and (in its most common form) a diatomic molecule.
- **It’s the most abundant element in the universe**, yet it’s rarely found free on Earth because it reacts readily with other elements.
- **Its physical properties** (low density, high speed of sound, low boiling point) make it ideal for high‑performance fuels and cryogenic applications.
- **Chemically, hydrogen is versatile**: it can act as an acid (proton donor) or a base (hydride donor), and it participates in a wide range of reactions from combustion to catalysis.
- **Safety**: While non‑toxic, hydrogen’s flammability and low ignition energy require careful handling.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
